description:
Hi, I'm Shuruthi, a 4th-year Aerospace Systems Engineering student joining the London virtual event. My interests are in aerodynamics and systems engineering, and I mostly work in MATLAB and CFD.

I'm planning to work on the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge, looking at how sunlight and Earth visibility vary between landing sites at the Moon's south pole.

 I'm always happy to chat or swap ideas, so feel free to say hello!
summary: Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive web app that lets mission planners, educators and the public compare Moon landing sites and dates in seconds. Users choose from curated sites (the south pole, CLPS landers, Apollo, Chandrayaan-3, Chang’e-6) or enter custom coordinates, then set a landing date and mission length. The tool shows Sun and Earth positions relative to the horizon. It reports the percentage of the mission with solar power, with direct-to-Earth communication and with both, plus the longest period of darkness and the time until sunset or Earthset. A site comparison table and a 90-day landing-date finder show how a schedule slip changes a mission’s chances. Sun and Earth positions computed with the IAU SOFA/ERFA models (epv00, moon98; Earth ephemeris fitted to JPL DE405) and the IAU/WGCCRE lunar orientation model. Landing-site coordinates are approximate, from published mission locations. No NASA datasets were accessed directly. Generative AI assisted development of site and demo.
details: The next stepLunar Landing Site Navigator is a browser-based tool that lets users compare Moon landing sites and dates in a few clicks. For any site and date it shows sunlight (power) availability, Earth visibility (direct-to-Earth comms), the longest darkness and the time until sunset or Earthset. It also includes a landing-date finder that shows how a schedule slip affects the mission. Positions are computed from IAU SOFA/ERFA ephemeris models and the IAU lunar orientation model, accounting for libration, Earth parallax, the Sun’s disc and the lack of atmosphere. The tool is built in Python and JavaScript, with its development assisted by generative AI. It aims to make south-pole mission planning faster for engineers and easier to understand for educators and the public. It’s a screening tool, and adding LOLA terrain data is the next key implementation.
